name: Cuba
card_headline: Nationwide blackouts, a US oil cutoff and Trump's talk of military force define Cuba, as record political imprisonment and emigration continue.
card_summary: Cuba's grid has collapsed island-wide at least six times in 2026 since the United States cut off oil in January. Washington has added sanctions, indicted Raul Castro and, on 12 November, Trump said he would consider force. Cuban officials denied in September that talks are under way. ECLAC projects a 6.5 percent contraction. Official data show 245,264 net departures in 2025, leaving 9.43 million people. Prisoners Defenders counts a record 1,281 political prisoners, and protests over power cuts recur.
card_local: elTOQUE reported at least five consecutive days of street protest in Havana in mid-May, with police vehicles deployed across the city. [1] CiberCuba relayed Justicia 11J's count of 775 political prisoners in April. [2]
card_international: AP and Reuters report that Cuba's grid has collapsed nationwide repeatedly since the US cut off oil in January, and Al Jazeera reports that Trump said on 12 November he would consider military force. [3][4] Euronews reports that the UN General Assembly's embargo vote fell to 130 in favor. [5]
card_scholar: Crisis Group (March) finds the crisis has domestic and US roots and proposes phased, reciprocal steps. [6] CSIS warns that US pressure could be miscalibrated into societal collapse. [7]
context_md: The US embargo on Cuba dates to 1960. [5] Raul Castro was president from 2008 to 2018 and remains influential, and Miguel Diaz-Canel is the current president. [8][9] The July 2021 protests were followed by the imprisonment of nearly 2,000 people, according to CSIS. [7] The economy has been under strain since Soviet-era subsidies ended in the early 1990s. [10] In January 2026 the United States seized Venezuela's president Nicolas Maduro, Venezuelan oil shipments to Cuba stopped, and Washington has since allowed only one tanker, from Russia, to dock. [3] The military-linked conglomerate GAESA dominates key sectors with little transparency, according to Freedom House. [11]

sections.title: The grid has collapsed nationwide at least six times this year, and the fuel to restart it is scarce
sections.body_md:
Cuba's electrical system failed across the whole island on 18 September. Al Jazeera, drawing on AFP and Reuters, called it at least the sixth nationwide blackout of 2026 and at least the 12th since late 2024. Cuban authorities told Reuters that a failure in high-voltage lines in the central region caused the collapse, and the state grid operator UNE also cited unstable weather. [12] The tally depends on the outlet: AP and Reuters called the 6 July outage the third of the year. [3]

Between collapses the cuts are long. In July, outages lasted more than 30 hours in parts of Havana and more than 70 hours in some rural areas, and a Havana resident said her neighborhood got three or four hours of power a day. [3] A Human Rights Watch researcher who visited Havana reported two or three hours a day in some neighborhoods. [10] In May, elTOQUE quoted the energy and mines minister saying that Russian fuel had run out and that the country had "absolutely no fuel oil or diesel." [1]

The supply break started in January. Before the crisis Mexico supplied about 44 percent of Cuba's oil imports and Venezuela 33 percent, and Cuba needs an estimated 100,000 barrels a day, according to Al Jazeera, which cited Kpler for stocks of 15 to 20 days at the end of January. [13] AP and Reuters report that Venezuelan deliveries stopped after the US removed Maduro and that Washington has since let only one Russian tanker dock. [3] The grid was already weak. Economist Ricardo Torres writes that generation fell from over 21,000 GWh in 2019 to under 16,000 GWh in 2025, with many main thermal plants more than 30 years old. [14] Crisis Group puts the crisis down to party rule, the embargo, mismanagement and long dependence on Venezuela. [6]

The health effects are the least counted part. ACAPS estimated in April that about nine million people were affected by fuel shortages. [15] CSIS reports that infant mortality rose from 4.8 to 6.8 per 1,000 births between 2012 and 2024 and that about 100,000 surgeries are postponed. [7] UN human rights experts warned in August of uncollected waste in parts of Havana and a risk of disease outbreaks. [16]

lenses.local: elTOQUE records the energy minister's admission that fuel oil and diesel had run out, and Prensa Latina, a state outlet, carried Diaz-Canel's line that an energy siege is asphyxiating Cuba. [1][17]
lenses.international: AP and Reuters, via Al Jazeera, link the repeated collapses to the January oil cutoff and to an aging grid. [3][12]
lenses.scholar: Ricardo Torres of the Cuba Study Group documents a decline in generation that predates the blockade, and ACAPS and CSIS document the humanitarian toll. [14][15][7]

sections.title: Washington has moved from embargo to an oil cutoff, indictments and public talk of force
sections.body_md:
In January, after the US seized Maduro, President Trump imposed what AFP calls a de facto energy blockade and threatened tariffs on countries that supply Cuba with fuel. [8][4] WOLA dates the tariff order to 29 January. [18] The term is contested. US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz denies that Cuba is under a blockade and blames its government for the suffering, while Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez calls the measures genocidal. [5][19]

The sanctions have widened. Executive Order 14404, signed on 1 May, authorizes blocking sanctions on persons in Cuba's energy, defense, mining, financial and security sectors and secondary sanctions on foreign banks. [20] OFAC's regulations took effect on 30 September, removed the authorization for accounts held solely by Cuban private entrepreneurs, and ended group people-to-people travel. [21] Washington has also sanctioned the state oil company, Diaz-Canel and relatives of Raul Castro, and a new round this month hit 10 people and entities. [4]

Legal and military signals have followed. A US grand jury indicted Raul Castro on 20 May over the 1996 shootdown of two Brothers to the Rescue planes, and Florida's attorney general obtained a state arrest warrant on 19 October. [22][8] Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in May that diplomacy was a low-probability path. [22] On 12 November Trump told a radio host he would consider military force and wants to "get Cuba done" before leaving office in 2029. In March the head of US Southern Command told senators that US troops were not rehearsing an invasion. [4]

Talks exist but are thin. Cuba confirmed meetings in Havana in April, and Reuters reported US proposals including Starlink access and compensation for seized property. [23] In September Rubio said Washington would deal with Cuban leaders whose "hands are not stained with blood," while Cuban officials denied that talks were under way. [19] 14ymedio reports that two Democratic congressmen asked Diaz-Canel to release more than 200 prisoners to unblock stalled talks, a claim from a single listing. [24] On 28 October the UN General Assembly voted 130 to 17 with 25 abstentions to call for an end to the embargo, the lowest support since 1995. [5]

lenses.local: 14ymedio's English edition reports on stalled talks and a possible release of more than 200 prisoners, but this rests on one listing page. [24]
lenses.international: AFP, AP and Reuters, as carried by Al Jazeera, report the indictments, sanctions rounds and Trump's 12 November remarks. [8][4]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's guests describe the policy as maximum pressure, with Michael Bustamante warning in the Journal of Democracy that economic collapse alone will not produce a legitimate transition, and Javier Corrales rating collapse unlikely while the military stays loyal. [25][26][27]

sections.title: The economy: a falling peso, a shrinking GDP and a private sector the US now targets
sections.body_md:
ECLAC projects that Cuba's economy will shrink 6.5 percent in 2026, the worst in the region, while economist Pedro Monreal projects a contraction of at least 15 percent, according to elTOQUE. [28] The Cuban government says the embargo cost it $8bn between March 2025 and February 2026, a figure that excludes the January energy restrictions and the May secondary sanctions. [19] Economist Julio Carranza wrote in December that GDP would end 2025 more than 12 points below its 2019 level, that hotel occupancy stayed below 20 percent and that the sugar harvest did not reach 200,000 tons. [29]

Prices and the peso tell the same story. Cumulative consumer price growth reached 7.18 percent by early May, against 6.56 percent a year earlier, and the dollar reached 535 pesos on elTOQUE's reference rate in April, up 45.4 percent from April 2025. [28] That rate reflects informal offers, not completed trades, and I found no later figure from a source I opened. 14ymedio reports that workers in Matanzas hold two jobs because wages no longer cover food. [24]

The private sector is both an escape valve and a new target. Parliament approved a reform package in June that lets private firms employ more than 100 workers. [9] The US then revoked the permission for Cuban private entrepreneurs to hold US bank accounts, and Diaz-Canel called the US stance on private business "all a lie, all a fallacy." [9] OFAC's September rules block funds in such accounts absent a specific license. [21] The State Department designated the military-linked conglomerate GAESA on 7 May, and Freedom House says GAESA diverts foreign-currency earnings away from public services. [20][11]

External income is shrinking too. Carnegie's Javier Corrales says the economy has contracted since about 2019, tourism collapsed after COVID and remittances remain a main lifeline. [27] ONEI data relayed by CiberCuba show 228,091 non-resident Cubans visited in 2025, down from 294,816 in 2024. [30] 14ymedio reports that emigrants are now the largest group of visitors while total arrivals fell sharply, with 29,376 visitors in October. [24]

lenses.local: elTOQUE tracks prices and the informal exchange rate, and OnCuba carries Julio Carranza's argument that the government's draft recovery program is not sufficient. [28][29]
lenses.international: AP reports the June reform package and the October US restrictions on private firms. [9]
lenses.scholar: Corrales of Amherst College sees an economy in structural decline sustained by remittances, and Freedom House points to GAESA's opacity. [27][11]

sections.title: Emigration: 245,000 net departures in 2025 and a population now below 9.5 million
sections.body_md:
Cuba's statistics office, ONEI, reported on 21 July that the island ended 2025 with 9,434,593 people. Net migration was negative by 245,264 people, about 2.5 percent of the population, in the ninth straight year of population loss. The natural growth rate was minus 7.1 per 1,000, so deaths exceed births. [31]

Wire and news copy still uses older numbers. NPR carried the figure of about 11 million in March, and Al Jazeera used about 11 million in February. [32][13] Al Jazeera, citing AP and Reuters, gave nearly 10 million and 9.6 million within one July article. [3]

Independent estimates of the outflow are higher than the official picture. Freedom House says roughly a quarter of the population has left in the past five years. [11] Crisis Group and WOLA both say more than one million Cubans have left since 2021. [6][18] I found no source that reconciles these counts with ONEI's.

Where people go has changed. WOLA says Cubans are now the third-largest group seeking asylum worldwide, most heading to Latin America or Spain as US options narrowed, and that more than 500,000 Cubans in the United States are at risk of detention and deportation. [18] CSIS warns that a collapse would trigger large-scale emigration and leave behind people without means to leave, including about 300,000 elderly people living alone. [7] Ties with those who left are loosening: CiberCuba reports that 23,002 emigrant visitors came in January and February 2026, against 38,597 a year earlier, and ONEI cites US measures, the internal crisis and flight cancellations. [30]

lenses.local: CiberCuba, using ONEI's retrospective data, reports falling visits by emigrants. [30]
lenses.international: EFE carries ONEI's population and net-migration figures. [31]
lenses.scholar: CSIS and Freedom House describe emigration as both a safety valve and a loss of workers, and WOLA documents the shift of destinations. [7][11][18]

sections.title: A record 1,281 political prisoners, a jailed editor and protests that police answer with arrests
sections.body_md:
Prisoners Defenders counted 1,281 political prisoners at the end of May, a new record, with 28 new detentions in the month and 2,076 recorded since 1 July 2021. [33] Justicia 11J counted 775 in April, 338 of them sentenced over the 11 July 2021 protests, so the counts differ with each group's method. [2] Freedom House puts the figure above 1,280 as of June. [11] On 2 April the government announced a pardon of 2,010 prisoners, but Human Rights Watch and Cuban groups had not identified any political prisoners among them, because the pardon excluded "crimes against authority." [34]

Press freedom is shrinking. The Committee to Protect Journalists reports that Henry Constantin, director of La Hora de Cuba, has been held since 16 September in Camagüey over an alleged "disobedience" charge, and that his lawyers say the law provides only a fine for missing a first summons. [35] 14ymedio reports that he remains jailed and that his partner was barred from visiting for three months. [24] Human Rights Watch says the government controls all media and censors independent journalists. [36]

Protest has become routine. In May, elTOQUE reported at least five consecutive days of protest in Havana, with blocked streets, burning trash, pot-banging and heavy police deployment. [1] In March, Reuters reported that protesters attacked a Communist Party office in Moron, and the state newspaper Invasor said five people were detained. [37] CSIS cites the Cuban Observatory of Conflicts for 1,245 protests in March, including 556 it classes as challenges to the police state. [7] Prisoners Defenders recorded 14 new political prisoners after protests in Antilla, Holguin, on 19 May. [33]

Organized opposition is thin. Crisis Group notes that no clear negotiator or opposition leader has emerged. [6] Corrales argues that the military's loyalty makes regime collapse unlikely. [27]

lenses.local: elTOQUE documents the May protests and the police response, and 14ymedio reports on Constantin's detention. [1][24]
lenses.international: Reuters, via bdnews24, reports the Moron riot and the state newspaper's account of the detentions. [37]
lenses.scholar: HRW, Freedom House and CPJ document the prisoner counts and press cases, and CSIS compiles protest data from the Cuban Observatory of Conflicts. [34][11][35][7]

timeline.text: The US embargo on Cuba begins after the revolution and the nationalization of US-owned property.
Mass protests on 11 July are followed by the imprisonment of nearly 2,000 people, according to CSIS.
Authorities release 553 detainees after talks involving the Vatican and the United States; Cuban NGOs estimate about 200 were political prisoners.
The US seizes Venezuela's president Maduro, Venezuelan oil shipments to Cuba stop, and Trump threatens tariffs on countries that supply Cuba with oil.
Protesters attack a Communist Party office in Moron after power cuts and food shortages.
An island-wide blackout hits Cuba, the third major outage in about four months, according to NPR.
The government announces a pardon of 2,010 prisoners that Human Rights Watch says did not identify any political prisoners.
US officials meet Cuban officials in Havana, according to Axios as cited by Al Jazeera; Cuba confirms the talks on 21 April.
Trump signs Executive Order 14404, which authorizes sanctions on Cuba's key economic sectors and secondary sanctions on foreign banks.
A US grand jury indicts Raul Castro over the 1996 shootdown of two Brothers to the Rescue planes.
The grid collapses across the whole island, at least the sixth nationwide blackout of 2026.
OFAC's Cuba Sanctions Regulations take effect and the authorization for private entrepreneurs' US bank accounts is removed.
Florida obtains a state arrest warrant for Raul Castro.
The UN General Assembly votes 130 to 17 with 25 abstentions against the US embargo.
Trump says he would consider military force against Cuba and wants to get Cuba done before leaving office in 2029.

scores.coverage_basis: AP, Reuters and AFP file on Cuba often in 2026, with a story for each nationwide blackout, sanctions round and Trump statement. [3][12][4] Think tanks including Crisis Group, CSIS and Carnegie published on Cuba this year, and independent Cuban outlets such as elTOQUE and CiberCuba publish daily. [6][7][27][1] Coverage concentrates on US policy and the blackouts, with less on prisoners, health outcomes and life outside Havana. [10]

severity.basis: There is no armed conflict, but Reuters reports a violent riot in Moron and the US has indicted Raul Castro and raised the possibility of force. [37][4]
ACAPS estimates nine million people affected by fuel shortages, and UN experts warn of a developing humanitarian crisis with disease risk. [15][16]
Prisoners Defenders counts a record 1,281 political prisoners and CPJ reports an editor jailed since September, while HRW says the government controls all media. [33][35][36]
ECLAC projects a 6.5 percent contraction, the informal dollar rose 45.4 percent in a year to April, and the US has widened sanctions to banks and private firms. [28][21]
Nationwide collapses came at least six times this year, US sanctions widened in May and September, and UN General Assembly support for Cuba fell to its lowest since 1995. [12][21][5]

parts.basis: The United States is escalating with sanctions, indictments and talk of force, and China says it firmly supports Cuba while Russia criticized the US approach. [4][22]
Cuba is a small, shrinking economy sustained by remittances, and its fuel need of about 100,000 barrels a day is small in world terms. [27][13]
More than one million Cubans have left since 2021 and CSIS warns that a collapse would trigger large-scale emigration. [6][7]
WOLA says over 500,000 Cubans in the US face a risk of detention and deportation, and Cubans are the third-largest group seeking asylum worldwide. [18]
UN human rights experts state that the US measures breach Article 2 of the UN Charter, and the Maduro seizure is cited by Trump and analysts as a model. [16][3]

summary: Cuba matters beyond its borders mainly through US policy, migration and the precedent of a US-engineered change of government after the Maduro seizure, since its own economic weight is small. [3][7] The score is held down by thin evidence of Russian or Chinese material support, which this draft found mostly as statements. [22]
gi.up: A US military strike, a government collapse or a mass maritime exodus would raise it.
gi.down: A negotiated deal that eases the oil cutoff and stabilizes the grid would lower it.

gaps: Local sourcing: Cubanet and Diario de Cuba could not be opened in this session, so they appear nowhere as sources; 14ymedio was read only through a Translating Cuba listing page (headlines and summaries), and Havana Times was seen only as a headline listing. Claims from 14ymedio (more than 200 prisoners discussed, Constantin's partner barred, emigrants as the largest visitor group, Matanzas workers, Mariel trade) rest on that single listing.

State media: Granma, Cubadebate, Juventud Rebelde and Prensa Latina were not read. The Prensa Latina page failed to open and is cited only for its headline and date, flagged state_affiliated. The official Cuban line comes from AP, AFP and Al Jazeera quotations.

Crisis Group was read through the ecoi.net mirror of its 2 March 2026 piece; the original on crisisgroup.org was not opened and no later Crisis Group output was found. The Carnegie items are podcasts, and no written Carnegie paper was found.
The CSIS paper has no date on the page (inferred as early April 2026), and its figures on poverty, protests and health come from third-party and Cuban sources I did not check.

Blackout counts differ between outlets and were not reconciled: AP and Reuters said third on 6 July, Al Jazeera said at least sixth on 18 September, and one aggregator listing said eight. No UNE megawatt deficit figure from an opened source is included.

Political prisoner counts differ by method (Prisoners Defenders 1,281 for May, Justicia 11J 775 for April); no Prisoners Defenders report after June was read. The 2,010-prisoner pardon was described only through HRW.

Economic figures rest on elTOQUE's relay of ECLAC and Pedro Monreal projections and on an official inflation figure; ECLAC's own document, any IMF or World Bank data, remittance totals and the later exchange rate were not opened. The elTOQUE exchange rate reflects informal offers.

Food security: no WFP, FAO or OCHA figures and no IPC-style analysis were read, so hunger is covered through ACAPS, CSIS and UN experts only. A report that the WHO chief visited Havana on 24 to 25 November appeared only in an Al Jazeera listing and is not used.
The Cubanet headline on the effect of the November US midterms on Cuba policy was seen but not opened, so the draft does not assess it.
Great-power stake rests on statements by China and Russia and on US actions; no source on Russian or Chinese deliveries, loans or bases was read.
No documentary, photo essay or film was verified for the media list. Books were verified through retailer or publisher listings, not reviews.
The Executive Order 14404 sanctions and the 5 November further designations were read through law-firm alerts and Al Jazeera, not the Federal Register or OFAC texts.
Cuban government statements on the embargo cost ($8bn) and on denial of talks were read only through Al Jazeera.

books.title: Cuba: A Brief History (Cuba: Una breve historia)
books.author: Sergio Guerra Vilaboy, with Mary Todd and Oscar Loyola Vega
books.why: A short history by Cuban authors that runs from the pre-Hispanic era to the 2018 succession and the reversal of US engagement under Trump.
books.label: Penguin Books Australia (Seven Stories Press)

books.title: Cuban Memory Wars: Retrospective Politics in Revolution and Exile
books.author: Michael J. Bustamante
books.why: Traces how Havana, Miami and ordinary Cubans remembered the revolution, which helps explain why every policy debate on Cuba is also a debate about the past.
books.label: Schweitzer (University of North Carolina Press)

books.title: Cuba Explained: Revolution, Sanctions, and Strategic Survival
books.author: Thomas R. Calder
books.why: A self-published structural history of modern Cuba, from sugar and Soviet support to cautious market reforms. Treat it as a secondary overview.
books.label: Books-A-Million (independently published)

podcasts.title: What Does the United States Want From Cuba?
podcasts.why: Bustamante describes the policy as maximum pressure and argues Cuba is not a failed state because the government keeps its monopoly on force.

podcasts.title: What to Know Before Trump Attacks Cuba
podcasts.why: Corrales weighs airstrikes, a leadership removal and a Venezuela-style deal, and says military loyalty makes collapse unlikely.

factchecks.claim: Cuba is not under a US blockade, and its people's suffering is the fault of their own government.
factchecks.by: Mike Waltz, US ambassador to the UN, at the General Assembly embargo debate on 28 October 2026
factchecks.evidence: AFP describes a de facto energy blockade imposed in January, and AP and Reuters report that Washington has allowed only one Russian tanker to dock since then. UN human rights experts call the measures a breach of the UN Charter. Crisis Group also attributes the crisis to party rule, mismanagement and dependence on Venezuela, so domestic policy is part of the cause. The legal label is contested, the fuel cutoff is documented.
